    YOUR POCKET FIELD GUIDE

    Inheritance, chance, and change.

    Rows and breeding jars

    Each row has room for eight beetles and has its own cycle counter. Choose two different living parents for a row’s jar, then Breed row. Only that row changes. Empty and unfinished jars leave their rows alone. Next generation advances all complete jars once; Play keeps making new broods from their original pairs. Saved jar parents remain until you replace or remove them, including when you switch activities. Repeated broods of the same parents are siblings, not successive descendant generations. Parents may come from any row; using the same pair in all jars explicitly prepares every population.

    Surprises inherited from parents

    Each beetle carries two inherited color recipes, and one can stay hidden. A baby receives one complete recipe from each parent. Those recipes can pass through grandchildren and later descendants. A hidden color can appear even when both parents look green. This works for every color family, with no fixed color dominance ranking.

    This original teaching model has six linked binary genes encoding each recipe’s color and expression strength, plus three numeric shade genes. The stronger inherited recipe supplies the base color; a tie uses parent A’s copy. Three shade genes vary each RGB channel across its full dark-to-bright range, so custom colors, black and white are genetically reachable. A beetle’s color name describes its actual appearance, which can differ from the base recipe. A green beetle might carry a weaker red recipe, for example. Two such parents can produce offspring expressing that red recipe if both pass it, a 25% chance before mutation. Shade genes determine the exact visible result. Other parents have different possibilities. These are independent chances, not guaranteed proportions in a row of eight.

    Try an inheritance cross selects two green carriers and turns mutation off. The offspring preview enumerates the four equally likely recipe transmissions and 64 shade transmissions, grouping duplicate RGB colors. Full stats reveals the actual recipe copies and their expression strengths; the simplified view keeps these details hidden.

    Mutation is separate

    Unusual offspring do not require mutation if their parents already carry the necessary copies. A mutation can also introduce a new copy: a binary switch flips, or a shade value changes by ±1–36 within 0–255. The rate applies independently to 18 inherited copies. Mutations do not aim for the environment. Genes that are no longer carried by any beetle do not return from an invisible archive; new mutation would be needed.

    Bird mode, breeding mode, or both

    In bird mode, every living beetle gets one independent survival roll. The bird may eat any number, including none or all. Each hunt uses fresh rolls, even after restarting with the same population seed. Survivors can breed across rows and habitat boundaries. Mating favors the eight surrounding leaves, including diagonals. Distance weights apply to each individual partner: adjacent beetles have weight 1, two rings away 0.25, three rings about 0.083, and progressively less farther away. A weighted draw chooses a distinct real survivor. Movement between unlike habitat patches is also less frequent; this reduces mixing without preventing cross-boundary breeding. Identical backgrounds mix freely. This invented movement rule uses actual background colors, not beetle color names. Offspring replace a surviving parent on its leaf, and nearby survivors refill vacant leaves. With no close partner, a farther survivor can mate instead. With at least two survivors on the whole board, their offspring fill all rows. One survivor stays on its original leaf without offspring; zero survivors leaves an empty board. No survivor quota or rescue reroll is used. Contrasting beetles are more likely to be eaten when selection is strong, with chance still involved. With the animation on, each beetle rolls when the bird reaches its leaf. The counter reports only completed checks; reproduction waits until all beetles have been checked. At zero selection strength, each insect has a 70% survival chance regardless of color. With stronger selection, better camouflage improves that insect’s chance. The same rule compares shade and color balance for every beetle and background; there is no preferred color name. Before the neighbor boost, full-strength survival is 10% + 80% × camouflage². Intermediate strength blends those two rules. The game then compares the eight surrounding leaves, including diagonals, on the same background. A beetle that blends in better than those neighbors gets a boost. More contrasting neighbors give greater protection; identical neighbors give none. This comparison uses the board at the start of the hunt, so the bird’s checking order does not change anyone’s odds. When all beetles match the background, their ordinary camouflage still keeps eating risk low. Chance remains, and each insect rolls once.

    In breeding mode, students choose parents, with no bird selection during that breeding step. When both activities are enabled, students may switch between choosing parents and watching natural selection. Jars always replace only their own rows. Turning off the bird animation hides the animation, while bird selection still operates.

    Neapolitan habitats

    Neapolitan is an additional environment alongside Meadow, Dry leaves, and Dusk. It divides the board’s leaf area into three continuous vertical color bands of equal width. Each insect is judged against the band behind its own leaf. With eight columns, the left three leaves are in the first third, the next two in the middle, and the right three in the last third. Jars are outside these survival zones. In bird mode, offspring stay near their parents. Nearby mating spans rows, columns, and diagonals, with lower distance weights per individual farther partner. Crossing between unlike habitat patches is less frequent but always possible. When equally near survivors refill an empty leaf, survivors from a similar habitat are more likely to supply its first parent. This lets matching colors gradually form bands while genes still move between zones. Colors are inherited and selected; the game never assigns offspring colors to match a band. Each beetle’s advantage uses the actual color under its leaf, including custom habitat colors. Chance and mutation can keep the bands mixed. In jar mode, offspring fill only their jar’s row.

    Classroom links

    Classroom setup lets the teacher allow breeding only, bird only, or both, and choose whether students can change the environment. Shared links apply these permissions and starting presets automatically. Uncheck Allow continuous Play to hide Play and let students advance one generation at a time. The teacher may show full stats, charts, genetics, and data downloads, or keep the simplified view. Activity and environment permissions remain in effect. Start over restores the assigned starting conditions; notes remain.

    Observe and record

    Changing an environment never recolors existing beetles. It changes which colors blend in. Pause, predict, and compare the next generations. Average camouflage is a color similarity score, not a survival probability; diversity measures color spread. The teacher chart combines all rows, while each row tracks its own generation.

    A simplified model

    These invented color recipes illustrate inherited variation, hidden alleles, linkage, natural selection, mutation, and drift. They do not claim to reproduce actual beetle color genetics. Each row has a capacity of eight, color genes travel together as a recipe, shade genes inherit independently, and survival depends on camouflage, nearby contrast, and chance.

    Drag with a mouse, trackpad, pen, or touch. With a keyboard, select a beetle and activate an empty jar slot. On small screens, swipe along a row. Save observations before leaving; all state stays in this browser tab.
